items.prose: A fund screens small-cap stocks for takeovers. Its records say 8% of screened stocks become targets. A rumour on a trading forum appears for 45% of eventual targets and for 6% of the other stocks.

parts.question: Imagine 5,000 screened stocks. How many of them are targets with a rumour?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Split the 5,000 by the base rate first, then apply 45% inside the targets.

byKey.all-targets: That is every target. Only 45% of them have a rumour.
byKey.rate-on-all: You applied 45% to all 5,000. It applies only inside the 400 targets.

explain.text: 8% of 5,000 is 400 targets. A rumour appears for 45% of them, which is 180 stocks.

parts.question: Using the 180 rumoured targets from part 1, how many of the 5,000 stocks have a rumour in all?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the rumoured targets to the rumoured stocks among the 4,600 others.

byKey.false-on-all: You applied 6% to all 5,000. It applies only to the 4,600 stocks that are not targets.
byKey.others-only: That is the false rumours alone. Add the 180 rumoured targets.

explain.text: The 4,600 other stocks give $4{,}600 \times 0.06 = 276$ false rumours. With the 180 true ones that is 456 rumoured stocks.

parts.question: A stock has a rumour. Using 180 and 456, what is the chance it is a target? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac{180}{456} \approx 0.3947$: most rumoured stocks are not targets.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the targets among the rumoured stocks only.

byKey.inverse: That is $P(\text{rumour} \mid \text{target})$. The question turns the condition round.
byKey.count-slip: You divided by 480 from the 6%-of-everyone slip. The rumoured stocks number 456.
byKey.over-false: You divided by the 276 false rumours. Divide by all 456 rumoured stocks.

explain.text: Of the 456 rumoured stocks, 180 are targets. So $P(\text{target} \mid \text{rumour}) = \tfrac{180}{456} \approx 0.3947$.

parts.question: Part 3 gave 0.3947, under one half, so the fund does not trade at today's base rate of 0.08. The fund trades a rumoured stock only when it is more likely a target than not. At what base rate would a rumoured stock be exactly as likely a target as not? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Make the rumoured targets equal the rumoured others, then solve for the base rate $b$.

byKey.no-complement: You set $0.45\,b = 0.06$. False rumours come from the share $1 - b$ that are not targets.
byKey.half: That is the chance after the rumour you want, not the base rate that gives it.
byKey.rate-gap: You subtracted the two rumour rates. Balance the two groups of rumoured stocks instead.

explain.text: Even chances need as many true rumours as false ones: $0.45\,b = 0.06\,(1 - b)$. That gives $0.51\,b = 0.06$, so $b \approx 0.1176$, well above today's 8%.

items.prose: A credit desk gives a company a 15% chance of a downgrade this year. A supplier delay shows up in 60% of downgrade years and 20% of other years. A finance director leaving shows up in 30% of downgrade years and 5% of others. Given the truth, the two arise independently.

parts.question: What are the prior odds of a downgrade, as the chance of a downgrade over the chance of none? Give one number: an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Odds put the chance of a downgrade over the chance of none.

byKey.probability: That is the probability. Odds divide it by the chance of no downgrade, 0.85.
byKey.reversed: You put the chance of no downgrade on top. Odds of a downgrade have it on the bottom.

explain.text: Odds compare the two outcomes: $\tfrac{0.15}{0.85} = \tfrac{3}{17} \approx 0.1765$, or 3 to 17.

parts.question: A supplier delay is reported. Starting from odds of $\tfrac{3}{17}$, what are the odds of a downgrade now? Give the odds as one number: an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: The likelihood ratio is $\tfrac{0.6}{0.2} = 3$, so the odds become $\tfrac{9}{17}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the delay's likelihood ratio and multiply the odds by it.

byKey.prob-times: You multiplied the probability 0.15 by 3. The ratio multiplies the odds, $\tfrac{3}{17}$.
byKey.inverse-lr: You divided by 3. A delay is likelier before a downgrade, so the odds go up.
byKey.rate-gap: You added the gap 0.6 - 0.2 to the odds. Evidence multiplies odds by a ratio.

explain.text: The delay is $\tfrac{0.6}{0.2} = 3$ times likelier in a downgrade year. So the odds become $\tfrac{3}{17} \times 3 = \tfrac{9}{17} \approx 0.5294$.

parts.question: Then the finance director leaves. Using odds of $\tfrac{9}{17}$ from part 2, what is the probability of a downgrade now? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: The odds become $\tfrac{9}{17} \times 6 = \tfrac{54}{17}$, so the chance is $\tfrac{54}{71} \approx 0.7606$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the odds by the exit's likelihood ratio, then turn odds into a probability.

byKey.odds: That is the odds, $\tfrac{54}{17}$. Turn it into a probability: $\tfrac{54}{54 + 17}$.
byKey.ratio-sum: You added the two ratios, 3 + 6, and applied 9 to the prior. Independent evidence multiplies: $3 \times 6 = 18$.
byKey.prob-slip: You carried 0.45 from part 2's slip as a probability. Start from odds of $\tfrac{9}{17}$.

explain.text: The exit's ratio is $\tfrac{0.30}{0.05} = 6$, so the odds become $\tfrac{54}{17}$. As a probability that is $\tfrac{54}{54 + 17} = \tfrac{54}{71} \approx 0.7606$.

parts.question: The desk cuts its holding once the chance of a downgrade reaches 0.95. From odds of $\tfrac{54}{17}$, how many more independent reports, each with ratio 3 like the delay, does it need?

feedback.correct: A chance of 0.95 is odds of 19. One report gives about 9.5 and two give about 28.6, so 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn 0.95 into odds first, then multiply $\tfrac{54}{17}$ by 3 until you pass it.

byKey.prob-as-odds: You compared the odds 3.18 with 0.95. A chance of 0.95 is odds of 19.
byKey.ninety: One report gives odds of 9.53, a chance of about 0.905. That is short of 0.95.

explain.text: A chance of 0.95 is odds of $\tfrac{0.95}{0.05} = 19$. From $\tfrac{54}{17} \approx 3.18$, one report gives 9.53 and a second gives 28.6. So the desk needs 2.

parts.question: The desk then learns the finance director left because of the supplier delay. How should it treat the two reports?

options.text: The exit partly repeats the delay, so 0.76 is too high
Both reports are true, so both ratios still apply
options.why: Both are true, but the exit followed from the delay. Multiplying both ratios counts the delay twice.

options.text: Drop both reports and go back to the prior of 0.15
options.why: The delay is still real evidence. Only the double counting has to go.

options.text: The exit is now explained, so it lowers the chance
options.why: An explained exit adds little, but it is no evidence against a downgrade.

feedback.correct: The exit was not independent of the delay, so its ratio of 6 double counts.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask whether the two reports are still separate pieces of evidence.

explain.text: The chained update needed the two reports to arise independently. The exit followed from the delay, so the 0.76 counts the delay twice and is too high.

items.prose: A desk routes resting orders through a broker. The broker's algorithm is passive with chance 0.5, neutral with chance 0.3 and aggressive with chance 0.2. A resting order fills with chance 0.3, 0.5 and 0.8 under each kind. Given the kind, orders fill independently.

parts.question: The first order fills. Before you know the kind, what was the chance of that fill? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weight each fill chance by the chance of its kind, then add.

byKey.average: You averaged 0.3, 0.5 and 0.8 equally. The kinds have chances 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2.
byKey.aggressive-only: That is the aggressive path alone. Add the passive and neutral paths too.

explain.text: Each kind gives a path to a fill: $0.15$, $0.15$ and $0.16$. Their total is $0.46$.

parts.question: Using 0.46 from part 1, what is the chance the algorithm is aggressive, given the fill? Give an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the aggressive path by the total chance of a fill.

byKey.not-normalised: That is prior times likelihood. Divide by 0.46 so the three chances add to 1.
byKey.likelihood: That is the chance of a fill if aggressive. The question asks the other way round.
byKey.average-slip: You divided by 0.533, part 1's equal average. The chance of a fill is 0.46.

explain.text: Prior times likelihood for aggressive is $0.2 \times 0.8 = 0.16$. Normalising by 0.46 gives $\tfrac{16}{46} \approx 0.3478$.

parts.question: A second order fills too. Start from the chances after part 2: $\tfrac{15}{46}$, $\tfrac{15}{46}$ and $\tfrac{16}{46}$. What is the chance the algorithm is aggressive now? Give an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: The products are 4.5, 7.5 and 12.8 (in 46ths), so aggressive has $\tfrac{12.8}{24.8} \approx 0.5161$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply each chance from part 2 by its fill chance, then normalise.

byKey.once: That is the chance after one fill. The second fill updates it again.
byKey.not-normalised: You multiplied $\tfrac{16}{46}$ by 0.8 and stopped. Divide by the total of all three products.

explain.text: The new products are $15 \times 0.3 = 4.5$, $15 \times 0.5 = 7.5$ and $16 \times 0.8 = 12.8$, all over 46. They add to 24.8, so aggressive has $\tfrac{12.8}{24.8} = \tfrac{16}{31} \approx 0.5161$.

parts.question: Using the chances after both fills, $\tfrac{45}{248}$, $\tfrac{75}{248}$ and $\tfrac{128}{248}$, what is the chance a third order fills? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weight each kind's fill chance by its chance after the two fills.

byKey.prior-weights: You weighted by the chances before any fill. Use the chances after both fills.
byKey.most-likely: You assumed the algorithm is aggressive. It is only likely, so weight all three kinds.
byKey.equal: You weighted the three kinds equally. Use $\tfrac{45}{248}$, $\tfrac{75}{248}$ and $\tfrac{128}{248}$.

explain.text: Add the paths to a fill, weighting by the updated chances: $\tfrac{13.5 + 37.5 + 102.4}{248} = \tfrac{153.4}{248} \approx 0.6185$. Two fills have raised the next fill's chance from 0.46.

items.prose: A price feed has bad ticks: 2% of its prints are errors. Filter A flags 95% of errors and 4% of good prints. Flagged prints go on to filter B, which flags 70% of errors and 1% of good prints. Given the truth, the two filters err independently.

parts.question: What is the chance a print is flagged by filter A? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the flagged errors to the flagged good prints.

byKey.errors-only: That is the flagged errors alone. Good prints are flagged too.
byKey.rates-added: You added the two rates. Weight each by the share of prints it applies to.
byKey.false-on-all: You applied 4% to every print. It applies only to the 98% that are good.

explain.text: Flagged errors make up $0.02 \times 0.95 = 0.019$ of prints and flagged good prints $0.98 \times 0.04 = 0.0392$. The total is $0.0582$.

parts.question: Using 0.0582 from part 1, a print is flagged by A. What is the chance it is an error? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac{0.019}{0.0582} \approx 0.3265$: two in three flags are good prints.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Put the flagged errors over all flagged prints.

byKey.inverse: That is $P(\text{flag} \mid \text{error})$. The question turns the condition round.
byKey.false-slip: You divided by 0.059 from part 1's slip. The flagged share is 0.0582.
byKey.specificity: That is the share of good prints A passes. It says nothing alone about a flagged print.

explain.text: Of the flagged share 0.0582, errors make up 0.019. So $P(\text{error} \mid \text{flag}) = \tfrac{0.019}{0.0582} \approx 0.3265$.

parts.question: Filter B flags the print as well. Starting from your answer to part 2, $\tfrac{0.019}{0.0582}$, what is the chance it is an error now? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: Odds $\tfrac{0.019}{0.0392} \times 70 \approx 33.9$, so the chance is about $0.9714$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn part 2 into odds, multiply by B's likelihood ratio, then turn back.

byKey.odds: That is the odds. Turn it into a probability: $\tfrac{33.9}{1 + 33.9}$.
byKey.product: You multiplied the chance by 0.7. Evidence updates the odds by the ratio $\tfrac{0.70}{0.01}$.
byKey.skipped-a: You started from the 2% base rate. After A's flag the starting chance is 0.326.

explain.text: After A the odds are $\tfrac{0.019}{0.0392} \approx 0.485$, and B's ratio is $\tfrac{0.70}{0.01} = 70$. The new odds are about 33.9, a chance of $\tfrac{33.9}{34.9} \approx 0.9714$.

parts.question: Picture 1,000,000 prints. How many good prints are flagged by both filters?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Start with the 980,000 good prints, then apply each filter's false-flag rate in turn.

byKey.a-only: That is the good prints A flags. B then flags only 1% of them.
byKey.all-prints: You applied both rates to all 1,000,000. They apply only to the 980,000 good prints.

explain.text: Of 980,000 good prints, A flags $980{,}000 \times 0.04 = 39{,}200$. B flags 1% of those, so 392 good prints pass both.

parts.question: The desk deletes every print both filters flag. Using 392 from part 4, what share of the deleted prints are good? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the errors both filters flag, then find the good prints' share of all deleted prints.

byKey.over-all: You divided by all 1,000,000 prints. The share is of the deleted prints only.
byKey.over-errors: You divided by the 13,300 errors. The deleted prints are the errors plus the good ones.
byKey.error-share: That is the share that are errors. The question asks for the good prints.

explain.text: Both filters flag $20{,}000 \times 0.95 \times 0.70 = 13{,}300$ errors. So good prints are $\tfrac{392}{13{,}692} \approx 0.0286$ of the deleted prints. That matches part 3, since $1 - 0.9714 = 0.0286$.
